# SurrealDB Sink

> Write messages from Iggy streams into SurrealDB over the HTTP API, bulk inserts split by the configured batch size.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/surrealdb/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/connectors/sinks/surrealdb.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The SurrealDB sink connector writes messages from Iggy streams into SurrealDB over the HTTP API. Each poll is split into chunks of at most `batch_size` messages, with one SurrealQL bulk `INSERT IGNORE ... RETURN NONE` for each chunk containing valid records. Every record gets a deterministic record id derived from stream, topic, partition, offset, and message id, so replaying the same identities leaves existing records untouched. Messages are not buffered across polls.

This page is a curated subset of the documentation. The canonical reference is the upstream [surrealdb_sink README](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/surrealdb_sink) in the `apache/iggy` repository.

## Configuration

Use the broker credentials and runtime setup from the [sink guide](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/sink#configuration). From the matching 0.10.0 Iggy checkout root, build the plugin:

```bash
cargo build --release -p iggy_connector_surrealdb_sink
```

Start a local SurrealDB instance with the credentials used below. This example stores SurrealDB data in memory:

```bash
docker run -d --name iggy-surrealdb -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 surrealdb/surrealdb:v3.1.4 start --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --user root --pass root memory
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
```

After the health request succeeds, save this connector file in the runtime's connector directory. Its plugin path assumes the runtime starts from the checkout root.

```toml
type = "sink"
key = "surrealdb"
enabled = true
version = 0
name = "SurrealDB sink"
path = "target/release/libiggy_connector_surrealdb_sink"
plugin_config_format = "toml"

[[streams]]
stream = "example_stream"
topics = ["example_topic"]
schema = "json"
batch_length = 1000
max_wait = "1s"
min_count = 1
consumer_group = "surrealdb_sink_connector"

[plugin_config]
endpoint = "127.0.0.1:8000"
namespace = "iggy"
database = "connectors"
table = "iggy_messages"
username = "root"
password = "root"
auto_define_table = true
batch_size = 1000
```

Create the Iggy resources and send a JSON message, then start the runtime as described in the sink guide:

```bash
./target/release/iggy --username iggy --password iggy stream create example_stream
./target/release/iggy --username iggy --password iggy topic create example_stream example_topic 1 none 1d
./target/release/iggy --username iggy --password iggy message send --partition-id 0 example_stream example_topic '{"event":"created","count":1}'
```

Query the stored records:

```bash
curl --fail --user root:root -H 'Accept: application/json' -H 'Surreal-NS: iggy' -H 'Surreal-DB: connectors' --data 'SELECT * FROM iggy_messages;' http://127.0.0.1:8000/sql
```

### Common Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| ------ | ---- | ------- | ----------- |
| `endpoint` | string | **required** | SurrealDB HTTP host and port, e.g. `127.0.0.1:8000`. Full `http://` / `https://` URLs also accepted |
| `namespace` | string | **required** | Namespace selected at startup |
| `database` | string | **required** | Database selected at startup |
| `table` | string | **required** | Target table. Must be a safe SurrealQL identifier |
| `username` / `password` | string | none | Both required unless `auth_scope = "none"` |
| `auth_scope` | string | `root` | `root`, `namespace`, `database`, or `none` |
| `use_tls` | bool | `false` | Use `https://` when `endpoint` has no scheme |
| `auto_define_table` | bool | `false` | Create missing namespace/database and a schemaless table. Requires `auth_scope = "root"` |
| `define_indexes` | bool | `false` | Define a non-unique stream/topic/partition/offset index. Requires metadata and only runs with automatic table definition |
| `batch_size` | u32 | `1000` | Maximum input records per insert chunk. `0` is raised to `1` |
| `payload_format` | string | `auto` | `auto`, `json`, `text`, `base64`, or `binary` (alias for `base64`) |
| `include_metadata` | bool | `true` | Store stream/topic/partition/offset/timestamp/schema fields |

The `include_headers`, `include_checksum`, and `include_origin_timestamp` flags also default to `true` and work independently of `include_metadata`. Retry and timeout options are `query_timeout` (`30s` per HTTP request), `max_retries` (`3` total write attempts, with `0` raised to `1`), `retry_delay` (`100ms`), and `max_retry_delay` (`5s`). Invalid duration strings log a warning and fall back to `1s`. Zero durations are accepted. The maximum delay is raised to the base delay if configured smaller. `verbose_logging` defaults to `false` and raises per-poll submission logs from debug to info. See the upstream [surrealdb_sink README](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/surrealdb_sink) for the full table.

Namespace, database and table names must start with an ASCII letter or underscore and contain only ASCII letters, digits and underscores. Endpoint URLs cannot contain credentials, a path beyond `/`, a query or a fragment. An explicit `http://` or `https://` scheme takes precedence over `use_tls`. Payload-format and authentication-scope names are case-insensitive. Unknown values prevent startup.

With root, namespace or database authentication, startup calls `/signin` and SQL requests use Basic authentication with the configured scope. Namespace/database users require pre-existing resources and `auto_define_table = false`. With `auth_scope = "none"`, credentials are ignored. The server must permit those unauthenticated operations. Automatic DDL uses `IF NOT EXISTS` and does not migrate existing definitions. The optional `<table>_iggy_offset_idx` index is not a uniqueness constraint. `define_indexes = true` with metadata disabled rejects startup. Without automatic DDL it only logs a warning and skips index creation.

## Stored Shape

Every submitted record contains `id`, `iggy_message_id`, `payload` and `payload_encoding`. `include_metadata` adds `iggy_stream`, `iggy_topic`, `iggy_partition_id`, `iggy_offset`, `iggy_timestamp` and `iggy_schema`. The checksum and origin timestamp have separate flags. `iggy_headers` appears only when enabled and nonempty.

Iggy message IDs, partition IDs, offsets, timestamps and checksums are stored as strings. Timestamps retain Iggy's microsecond values, not SurrealDB datetime values. Record IDs encode stream/topic UTF-8 bytes as hex, then append partition, offset and the 32-digit hexadecimal message ID. Changing the payload or transforms does not change that identity. Changing any identity component creates a different key.

Payload formatting operates after the runtime decoder and transforms:

| `payload_format` | Stored payload and encoding |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- |
| `auto` | JSON values as `json`. Text/Proto variants as `text`. Raw/Avro/FlatBuffer bytes as `base64`, even when raw bytes contain valid JSON |
| `json` | A JSON value, parsing other payload variants as JSON. Invalid JSON is rejected |
| `text` | A string, decoding other payload bytes as UTF-8. Invalid UTF-8 is rejected |
| `base64` / `binary` | Base64 of the payload bytes, with `payload_encoding = "base64"` |

Non-raw headers are stored as strings, including numbers and booleans. Raw headers use `{"data":"AQID","iggy_header_encoding":"base64"}`. Payload JSON is sent as SurrealQL values, so destination schema, numeric and other value constraints still apply.

## Delivery Semantics

The runtime auto-commits while polling, logs/counts plugin callback failures, and continues without replaying the failed batch. The sink retries transaction-conflict errors, connection/timeouts, and HTTP 408, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504. Delays use capped exponential backoff with jitter. `Retry-After` is not used. Connection errors trigger reconnection and repeat sign-in/health/optional DDL. A failed reconnect stops that chunk, and retries plus startup requests can exceed `query_timeout` in total.

A malformed record is skipped while valid records in its chunk are still submitted. A failed chunk does not stop later chunks, and the last error is returned. The sink checks HTTP and SQL statement statuses. Its own processed counter counts records submitted in successful statements, including records ignored by `INSERT IGNORE`. Runtime counters instead reflect whether the whole callback succeeded. Neither is a count of newly inserted rows.

[SurrealQL `INSERT IGNORE`](https://surrealdb.com/docs/reference/query-language/statements/insert#ignoring-duplicates) preserves existing records with the same ID, including their old payloads. With the SurrealDB 3.1.4 instance above, `IGNORE` also silently skips unique-index conflicts and field-assertion failures while accepting valid records from the same chunk. These skips return a successful statement and are included in processed counters. This protects repeated writes of the same identities. It does not ensure that a failed batch will be delivered. There is no end-to-end at-least-once guarantee.

## Transforms

Transforms can be applied before writing to SurrealDB. See the [transforms documentation](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/transforms) for the available types and their configuration.

---

# BigQuery

> Write Iggy messages to an existing BigQuery table through the Storage Write API.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/bigquery/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/connectors/sinks/bigquery.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The BigQuery sink writes Arrow record batches through the Storage Write API `_default` stream. The target table must already exist. Startup reads its schema and rejects unsupported column types before consuming messages.

## Configuration

Build `iggy_connector_bigquery_sink` with the same release source as the runtime. Add this connector file to the [local provider](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/runtime#local-file-provider), then set your project, dataset and table:

```toml
type = "sink"
key = "bigquery"
enabled = true
version = 0
name = "BigQuery sink"
path = "target/release/libiggy_connector_bigquery_sink"
verbose = false

[[streams]]
stream = "example_stream"
topics = ["example_topic"]
schema = "json"
batch_length = 1000
consumer_group = "bigquery_sink_connector"

[plugin_config]
project_id = "my-project"
dataset = "iggy"
table = "events"

mode = "mapped"


include_metadata = true
include_headers = false

missing_value = "default"

max_request_bytes = 8388608
max_retries = 3
retry_delay = "1s"
max_retry_delay = "30s"
timeout = "30s"
verbose_logging = false
```

With metadata enabled, the table needs `iggy_stream` and `iggy_topic` as STRING, `iggy_partition_id` and `iggy_offset` as INT64, `iggy_timestamp` as TIMESTAMP and `iggy_id` as STRING. `include_headers=true` also needs `iggy_headers` as JSON or STRING.

## Credentials

Set either `credentials_path` or `credentials_json`, never both. Without either, the connector uses Application Default Credentials. The identity needs table schema read and row append permissions, `bigquery.tables.get` and `bigquery.tables.updateData`.

The optional `emulator_endpoint` and `emulator_grpc_endpoint` must be supplied together. They disable credentials and use plaintext connections. Use them only for local test services.

## Row mapping

In `mapped` mode, each payload must be a JSON object. Top-level fields map to table columns by name. Unknown fields are ignored. Required columns without defaults must have non-null values. Missing or null repeated columns become empty arrays.

In `raw` mode, `payload_column` defaults to `payload`. A JSON column requires valid JSON. A STRING column requires text or UTF-8 bytes. A BYTES column accepts raw bytes from any payload type. Other required columns must have defaults.

NUMERIC and BIGNUMERIC values must fit the declared precision and scale without rounding. Strings preserve decimal precision when JSON floating-point values cannot. INTERVAL and RANGE columns are unsupported.

## Batching and failures

`max_request_bytes` defaults to 8 MiB and is clamped from 64 KiB through 9 MiB. The sink splits batches to stay below the API request limit. `max_retries` defaults to three total attempts, including the first. Retry delay starts at one second and is capped at 30 seconds. Each request and startup operation has a 30-second default timeout.

A row that cannot be encoded or accepted is logged and dropped while other rows can proceed. Transient request failures retry with jittered exponential backoff. The `_default` stream does not provide exactly-once append semantics. A lost response can lead to duplicate rows.

The runtime commits offsets on read and does not replay a failed sink callback. A successful processed count does not prove that every row reached BigQuery. Preserve Iggy metadata when downstream deduplication or reconciliation is required. See the [source reference](https://github.com/apache/iggy/blob/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/bigquery_sink/README.md) for type mappings and row-error handling.

---

# RabbitMQ

> Send Iggy messages to RabbitMQ with the connector runtime.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/rabbitmq/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/connectors/sinks/rabbitmq.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The RabbitMQ sink publishes messages to an AMQP 0.9.1 exchange. It declares the configured exchange, enables publisher confirmations and uses mandatory publishing. Configure a queue and binding that match the routing key before sending messages.

## Configuration

Use the [sink runtime setup](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/sink) and build `iggy_connector_rabbitmq_sink`. Its plugin configuration is:

```toml
[plugin_config]
amqp_url = "amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672"
exchange = "iggy_events"
exchange_type = "topic"
routing_key = "iggy.messages"
durable_exchange = true
delivery_mode = "persistent"
include_metadata = true
verbose_logging = false
max_retries = 3
retry_delay_secs = 1
max_retry_delay_secs = 5
timeout_secs = 30
```

Use the guest credentials only with a local broker. Exchange type accepts `direct`, `topic`, `fanout` or `headers`. Exchange durability must match an existing exchange. Delivery mode accepts `persistent` or `non_persistent`. Durable delivery also depends on the broker and queue configuration.

## Headers and failure handling

User headers are preserved. With metadata enabled, the sink also adds `iggy_stream`, `iggy_topic`, `iggy_partition_id` and `iggy_offset`. String headers become AMQP LongString and raw headers become ByteArray.

The sink pipelines publishes and waits for confirmations. Transient failures retry from the first unconfirmed message. An in-flight tail can already be delivered, so retries can duplicate it. An unroutable mandatory publish fails the batch and forces a new connection before the next poll.

The runtime commits Iggy offsets on read and does not replay a failed callback after its retry budget. Publisher confirmations do not provide an end-to-end exactly-once guarantee. See the [source reference](https://github.com/apache/iggy/blob/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/rabbitmq_sink/README.md).

---

# Redshift

> Send Iggy messages to Redshift with the connector runtime.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/redshift/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/connectors/sinks/redshift.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The Redshift sink serializes batches to Parquet, stages them in S3 and loads an existing Redshift table with COPY. Configure both the Redshift connection and S3 access before starting the runtime.

## Configuration

Use the [sink runtime setup](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/connectors/sinks/sink) and build `iggy_connector_redshift_sink`. The plugin requires `connection_string`, `target_table`, `aws_iam_role`, `s3_bucket`, `s3_prefix` and `aws_region`. Supply S3 credentials through the supported credential configuration for your deployment.

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `batch_size` | 100 | Messages buffered per Parquet file and COPY operation |
| `max_connections` | 5 | Redshift connection pool size |
| `include_metadata` | `true` | Include stream, topic, partition, offset, timestamp and schema |
| `include_checksum` | `false` | Include the Iggy checksum |
| `include_origin_timestamp` | `false` | Include producer time |
| `payload_format` | `varbyte` | Payload encoding in Parquet |
| `max_retries` | 3 | COPY retries after the first attempt |
| `retry_delay` | One second | Pause between attempts |
| `archive` | `false` | Retain successfully loaded staging files under the archive prefix |

`aws_access_key_id` and `aws_secret_access_key` supply explicit staging credentials. `s3_endpoint` supports an alternate S3 endpoint. The [complete example configuration](https://github.com/apache/iggy/blob/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/redshift_sink/config.toml) includes a local staging service setup. Replace its credentials and role before use.

## Payloads and delivery

`payload_format="json"` writes a string column, not a native Redshift SUPER value. Use Redshift JSON parsing when structured queries need that representation. `varbyte` preserves the serialized payload as bytes.

With `archive=false`, a successfully loaded staging file is deleted. With it enabled, the file is moved under the archive prefix. A staged file alone does not prove that COPY completed.

The runtime commits offsets on read. A COPY failure that outlasts plugin retries is logged and is not replayed by the runtime. A retry after an uncertain load can duplicate rows. See the [source reference](https://github.com/apache/iggy/blob/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/connectors/sinks/redshift_sink/README.md).

---

# Introduction

> The official Iggy client SDKs, their packages and registries, and the transports each one supports.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/introduction/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/introduction.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

Iggy provides official client SDKs in multiple languages. The **Rust SDK** is the most feature-complete, offering both a high-level API (with auto-batching, consumer groups, offset management, retry logic) and a low-level API for direct protocol operations.

| Language | Package | Registry | Transport | Connection string |
|----------|---------|----------|-----------|-------------------|
| Rust | [iggy](https://crates.io/crates/iggy) | crates.io | TCP, QUIC, HTTP, WebSocket | Yes |
| Python | [apache-iggy](https://pypi.org/project/apache-iggy/) | PyPI | TCP, QUIC, HTTP, WebSocket | Yes (PyO3 wrapper) |
| Java | [iggy](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/org.apache.iggy/iggy) | Maven Central | TCP, HTTP | Yes |
| Node.js | [apache-iggy](https://www.npmjs.com/package/apache-iggy) | npm | TCP | Yes |
| Go | [iggy-go](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/apache/iggy/foreign/go) | pkg.go.dev | TCP | Yes |
| C# | [Apache.Iggy](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Apache.Iggy/) | NuGet | TCP, HTTP | Yes |
| C++ | [iggy-cpp](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/foreign/cpp) | GitHub (WIP) | TCP, QUIC, HTTP, WebSocket | Yes (Rust FFI) |
| PHP | [apache/iggy-php](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/foreign/php) | GitHub (source) | TCP, QUIC, HTTP, WebSocket | Yes (Rust FFI) |
| Swift | [Iggy](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/foreign/swift) | Swift Package Manager | TCP with optional TLS | Yes |

Python, C++, and PHP wrap the Rust SDK, so they inherit all transport protocols when using connection strings. Java and C# implement TCP and HTTP natively. Go and Node.js currently support TCP *only*.

The Rust SDK is always the first to receive new features.

## Server compatibility

Server 0.10.0 uses binary protocol 0.12.0. Upgrade clients and server together. There is no fallback to the 0.9 protocol. These are the component versions prepared for the upcoming release. Until publication, build the matching source release candidate.

| Component | Server 0.10.0 | Server 0.9.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust SDK (`iggy`) | `0.12.0` | `0.11.0` |
| CLI (`iggy-cli`) | `0.15.0` | `0.14.0` |
| Python SDK (`apache-iggy`) | `0.10.0` | `0.9.0` |
| Java SDK (`org.apache.iggy:iggy`) | `0.10.0` | `0.9.0` |
| Node.js SDK (`apache-iggy`) | `0.11.0` | `0.10.0` |
| Go SDK (`github.com/apache/iggy/foreign/go`) | `v0.10.0` | `v0.9.0` |
| C# SDK (`Apache.Iggy`) | `0.10.0` | `0.9.0` |
| Swift SDK | `0.2.0` | Not included |
| C++ SDK | `0.2.0`, source | Source |
| PHP SDK | `0.2.0`, source | Source |

C++ and PHP are included in the source archive. Swift uses the root Swift Package Manager manifest. See [Upgrading](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/server/upgrading) before replacing an existing deployment.

## Prerequisites

The examples below use the `iggy`/`iggy` root credentials. For a new local development instance, with no `IGGY_ROOT_USERNAME` or `IGGY_ROOT_PASSWORD` overrides, use:

```bash
cargo run --bin iggy-server -- --fresh --with-default-root-credentials
```

`--fresh` **wipes this replica's local data directory**. In a cluster, it can recover stored credentials from another replica. The environment takes precedence over the default-credentials flag, and bootstrap settings do not replace recovered credentials. This setup is for *development only*. Use a disposable data directory. See [Connection Strings](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/connection-strings) for the authentication details.

## Connection string

Every SDK has connection-string support. Accepted schemes, credentials and options differ by language. Java currently accepts username/password TCP strings with `tls` and `tls_ca_file` only. They provide a compact way to configure the client, including the transport protocol, credentials, server address, and options.

**Format:**

```text
iggy://username:password@host:port[?options]
```

**Transport selection** via scheme:

| Scheme | Transport |
|--------|-----------|
| `iggy://` | TCP (default) |
| `iggy+tcp://` | TCP |
| `iggy+quic://` | QUIC |
| `iggy+http://` | HTTP |
| `iggy+ws://` | WebSocket |

**Personal Access Token** authentication: any credential without a colon is treated as a PAT. Server-minted tokens carry no prefix, so paste the token exactly as returned:

```text
iggy://<personal-access-token>@host:port
```

**Examples:**

The Rust snippets assume an async Tokio context. HTTP requires an explicit login after construction. Connection-string credentials are applied automatically only by the binary transports.

```rust
use iggy::prelude::*;

// Rust - TCP with default options
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")?;

// Rust - QUIC
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy+quic://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8080")?;

// Rust - TCP with options
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string(
    "iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090?nodelay=true&reconnection_retries=unlimited&heartbeat_interval=5s"
)?;
```

```python
from apache_iggy import IggyClient

client = IggyClient.from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")
```

The option keys differ per transport and unknown keys are rejected as **hard errors**. See [Connection Strings](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/connection-strings) for the full per-transport option tables, defaults, and default ports.

## Common operations

The Rust SDK exposes these operations through traits on `IggyClient`. Availability and method names vary across foreign SDKs and transports:

- **SystemClient** - ping, stats, snapshot
- **StreamClient** - create, get, list, update, delete streams
- **TopicClient** - create, get, list, update, delete topics
- **PartitionClient** - create, delete partitions
- **SegmentClient** - delete segments
- **MessageClient** - send, poll messages
- **ConsumerOffsetClient** - get, store, delete consumer offsets
- **ConsumerGroupClient** - create, get, list, delete consumer groups
- **UserClient** - create, get, list, update, delete users, change password, update permissions
- **PersonalAccessTokenClient** - create, list, delete PATs
- **ClusterClient** - cluster metadata

## Polling strategies

When polling messages, you can choose from several strategies (Rust method names are shown):

| Strategy | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `offset(n)` | Start from a specific offset |
| `timestamp(t)` | Start at or after the given broker append timestamp |
| `first()` | Start from the earliest available message |
| `last()` | Read the tail ending at the committed offset, up to the requested count |
| `next()` | Continue after the stored consumer offset, or start at zero if none is stored |

## Partitioning strategies

When sending messages, you can control partition routing (Rust method names are shown):

| Strategy | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `partition_id(n)` | Send to a specific partition |
| `balanced()` | Round-robin across partitions |
| `messages_key(key)` | Hash-based routing by key |

The Rust SDK resolves these strategies before sending a binary request. The HTTP API can resolve the strategy on the server. Binary clients route to the selected partition primary.

## Read and recovery APIs

Use [deferred polling](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/deferred-polling) to wait for messages. A partition reader groups partitions by primary, and a consumer hands messages to the application one at a time. `PollOptions` defines the count, wait, byte budget and commit policy. Manual commits are the shared default.

Resource creation accepts typed options. Updates use patches that change only supplied fields and can reset supported defaults. See [Topic options](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/server/topic-options) and [Stream options](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/server/stream-options).

SDKs also expose [metadata changes](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/metadata-changes) and raw requests to a selected replica. Recovery APIs differ. Swift does not expose retained mutation resolution or pending mutation limits. It has abandonment for uncertain committing reads. Read each language guide before implementing retries after an uncertain write.

---

# Connection Strings

> The canonical reference for Iggy connection strings, covering every scheme, credential form and option.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/connection-strings/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/connection-strings.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

A connection string configures an Iggy client in a single line: transport, credentials, server address, and options. This page is the canonical reference for every scheme, credential form, and option key.

The tables below describe the Rust SDK and its Python, C++ and PHP bindings. Native Go, Node.js, C# and Swift clients also accept TCP connection strings. Java supports a smaller subset, described below.

## Format

```text
iggy[+transport]://credentials@host:port[?option=value&option=value]
```

The host and port are **always required**. Use a hostname, IPv4 address or bracketed IPv6 address such as `[::1]:8090`. Options are appended as `key=value` pairs separated by `&`. Scheme names and option keys are case-sensitive.

The parser does not percent-decode credentials or option values. Reserved separators such as `:` and `@` cannot be escaped inside a username or password. Use a PAT for credentials that contain them. Duplicate option keys use the last value. Boolean options enable only for the literal `true`. Use `false` to disable them.

**Unknown option keys are hard errors.** The parser rejects the whole string with `InvalidConnectionString` instead of ignoring the key, so a typo fails fast rather than silently falling back to a default.

## Transport selection

The scheme picks the transport. Each transport has its own default server port:

| Scheme | Transport | Default server port |
|--------|-----------|---------------------|
| `iggy://` | TCP (default) | 8090 |
| `iggy+tcp://` | TCP | 8090 |
| `iggy+quic://` | QUIC | 8080 |
| `iggy+http://` | HTTP | 3000 |
| `iggy+ws://` | WebSocket | 8092 |

## Credentials

Two forms are accepted:

**Username and password**, separated by a colon. Both parts must be non-empty:

```text
iggy://username:password@127.0.0.1:8090
```

**Personal Access Token**: any credential without a colon is treated as a PAT. Server-minted tokens are plain base64 strings with no prefix, so paste the token exactly as the server returned it:

```text
iggy://<personal-access-token>@127.0.0.1:8090
```

**Do not prepend anything** to the token. Strings like `iggypat-...` appear only in Iggy's own test code. A real token with a prefix added will fail to log in.

The examples use `iggy`/`iggy`. For a new local development instance, with no `IGGY_ROOT_USERNAME` or `IGGY_ROOT_PASSWORD` overrides, use:

```bash
cargo run --bin iggy-server -- --fresh --with-default-root-credentials
```

The environment takes precedence over the flag. Stored or recovered root credentials are not replaced by bootstrap settings. `--fresh` deletes this replica's local data. In a cluster it can recover committed state, including credentials, from another replica. Use this reset only for disposable development data. A fresh standalone server requires credentials. Provision root credentials on every replica for a new cluster.

TCP, QUIC, and WebSocket apply connection-string credentials during `connect()`. HTTP requires an explicit login, as described below.

## Duration values

Options typed as durations take human-readable values such as `5s`, `500ms`, or `1m`, unless a table below says the value is a plain number. Heartbeat and reconnection intervals must be greater than zero. The reconnection cooldown can be zero.

## TCP options

| Key | Description | Default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| `tls` | Enable TLS (`true`/`false`) | `false` |
| `tls_domain` | Name for TLS validation. When empty, use the dialed hostname or IP | empty |
| `tls_ca_file` | PEM file of trusted CA certificates, replacing the built-in roots | none |
| `reconnection_retries` | Retry passes over known endpoints after the initial pass, or `unlimited` | `unlimited` |
| `reconnection_interval` | Base of exponential backoff with full jitter, capped at ten seconds | `1s` |
| `reestablish_after` | Stable connection duration that resets retry backoff | `5s` |
| `heartbeat_interval` | Duration between heartbeats | `5s` |
| `nodelay` | Enable `TCP_NODELAY` (`true`/`false`) | `false` |

```text
iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090?tls=true&tls_domain=localhost&tls_ca_file=core/certs/iggy_ca_cert.pem&reconnection_retries=5&heartbeat_interval=3s&nodelay=true
```

With `tls=true`, TCP always validates the server certificate. Without `tls_ca_file`, it uses the built-in Mozilla roots. An explicit CA file can trust a private CA. The example above runs from the repository root against a TLS-enabled listener using the test certificate and key in `core/certs/iggy_cert.pem` and `core/certs/iggy_key.pem`. Those certificates are for local testing. See [Security](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/server/security) for TLS configuration.

## QUIC options

The QUIC reconnection keys **differ from TCP**: `reconnection_max_retries` (not `reconnection_retries`) and `reconnection_reestablish_after` (not `reestablish_after`). Using the TCP names in a QUIC string is a hard error.

| Key | Description | Default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| `response_buffer_size` | Maximum bytes read for one response | Protocol maximum record reply size |
| `max_concurrent_bidi_streams` | Maximum concurrent peer-initiated bidirectional streams | `10000` |
| `datagram_send_buffer_size` | Datagram send buffer size in bytes | `100000` |
| `initial_mtu` | Initial UDP payload size in bytes, clamped to at least `1200` | `1200` |
| `send_window` | Send window size in bytes | `100000` |
| `receive_window` | Connection receive window size in bytes | `100000` |
| `keep_alive_interval` | Keep-alive interval in milliseconds. `0` disables it | `5000` |
| `max_idle_timeout` | Idle timeout in milliseconds. `0` leaves Quinn's `30000` ms default | `10000` |
| `validate_certificate` | Validate the server certificate (`true`/`false`) | `false` |
| `heartbeat_interval` | Duration between heartbeats | `5s` |
| `reconnection_max_retries` | Number of reconnection attempts, or `unlimited` | `unlimited` |
| `reconnection_interval` | Duration between reconnection attempts | `1s` |
| `reconnection_reestablish_after` | Stable connection duration that resets retry backoff | `5s` |

```text
iggy+quic://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8080?validate_certificate=false&reconnection_max_retries=5
```

QUIC certificate validation is disabled by default. When enabled, it uses the platform verifier and the connection-string configuration's server name, `localhost`. For a different certificate name, use the Rust QUIC configuration builder's `with_server_name()` method. Values above QUIC's 62-bit limit for `max_concurrent_bidi_streams`, `receive_window`, or `max_idle_timeout` are rejected with `InvalidConfiguration`.

## WebSocket options

| Key | Description | Default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| `heartbeat_interval` | Duration between heartbeats | `5s` |
| `reconnection_retries` | Number of reconnection attempts, or `unlimited` | `unlimited` |
| `reconnection_interval` | Duration between reconnection attempts | `1s` |
| `reestablish_after` | Stable connection duration that resets retry backoff | `5s` |
| `read_buffer_size` | Read buffer size in bytes | `131072` |
| `write_buffer_size` | Target write buffer size in bytes | `131072` |
| `max_write_buffer_size` | Maximum write buffer size in bytes. Must exceed `write_buffer_size` | `usize::MAX` |
| `max_message_size` | Maximum incoming WebSocket message size in bytes | `67108864` |
| `max_frame_size` | Maximum incoming frame payload size in bytes | `16777216` |
| `accept_unmasked_frames` | Has no effect on client connections | `false` |
| `tls` | Enable TLS (`true`/`false`) | `false` |
| `tls_domain` | Name for TLS validation. When empty, use the connected IP | empty |
| `tls_ca_file` | PEM file of trusted CA certificates when validation is enabled | none |
| `tls_validate_certificate` | Validate the server certificate (`true`/`false`) | `false` |

```text
iggy+ws://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8092?heartbeat_interval=5s&max_message_size=1048576
```

WebSocket TLS does not validate the server certificate unless `tls_validate_certificate=true`. With validation enabled, `tls_ca_file` replaces the built-in Mozilla roots. Size limits cannot be removed through connection strings. Use the WebSocket configuration object for an unlimited message or frame size.

## HTTP options

| Key | Description | Default |
|-----|-------------|---------|
| `heartbeat_interval` | Duration between heartbeats | `5s` |
| `retries` | Maximum retries for transient request failures | `3` |

```text
iggy+http://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:3000?retries=5
```

The HTTP scheme constructs a plain `http://` API URL. Use the Rust HTTP builder's `with_api_url()` for HTTPS. HTTP parses the credential field but does not log in with it. In Rust, call `login_user()` or `login_with_personal_access_token()` explicitly before protected requests.

## Usage

In Rust, construct clients inside a Tokio runtime, which QUIC needs even before `connect()`. The following snippet assumes an async function returning `Result<_, IggyError>` and the matching [Rust SDK setup](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/intro).

```rust
use iggy::prelude::*;

// TCP with default options
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")?;

// QUIC
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy+quic://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8080")?;

// WebSocket
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy+ws://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8092")?;

// HTTP
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy+http://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:3000")?;
client.login_user("iggy", "iggy").await?;
```

```python
from apache_iggy import IggyClient

client = IggyClient.from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")
```

When you need settings a connection string cannot express (client-side encryption, a custom `Partitioner`, and similar), start from `IggyClientBuilder::from_connection_string()` and extend the builder on top.

## Pending-operation limits

Rust binary transport strings accept `max_pending_operations` and `max_pending_operation_bytes`. Defaults are 256 operations and 67108864 bytes. Both must be positive. The byte budget includes frozen headers and bodies, so it must fit the largest mutation you need to send.

Committing fetches use a separate pool with the same configured limits. That pool stores target metadata, not reply bodies, and retains unknown progress across sessions. Exhausting a limit rejects or delays further work according to the operation path. See [Client failover](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/clustering/client-failover).

## Native SDK differences

Java accepts only TCP schemes, username/password credentials, `tls` and `tls_ca_file`. It rejects PAT connection strings and other options. Go's `client.ParseConnectionString` returns options for `client.WithTcp`. Node.js constructors accept a string except `SimpleClient`, which wraps an existing raw client. C# exposes its connection-string factory described in the [C# guide](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/csharp/guide).

Swift accepts the TCP option names, but checks and then ignores pending mutation limits because it has no retained mutation pool. Its reconnect interval is a full pause between endpoint rounds. Node.js accepts `reestablish_after` for format compatibility without applying a Node equivalent. Do not assume one SDK's parser and timing behavior across all languages.

---

# Deferred Polling

> Wait for messages, read several partitions and choose when to store consumer offsets.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/deferred-polling/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/deferred-polling.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

Deferred polling lets the server wait for messages before answering a read. The read returns when enough messages are available or its wait ends. A quiet partition does not need a repeated request loop.

## Choose read limits

`PollOptions` separates read limits from the polling strategy and consumer identity. A strategy selects the starting position, such as a specific offset or the next stored offset.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `count` | 1000 | Maximum messages in one read |
| `max_wait` | Zero | Zero returns immediately. A positive duration enables waiting |
| `min_count` | 1 | Messages needed to finish the wait early, from 1 through `count` |
| `max_bytes` | 1 MiB | Reply budget, including binary metadata and batch framing |
| `commit` | Manual | When to store the returned position |

These are the shared poll defaults. High-level consumers can select a positive wait by default. The SDK derives a request timeout from the wait plus 10 seconds. The wire protocol permits waits up to 600 seconds, but the server caps them at `sharding.deferred_poll_max_wait`, 30 seconds by default.

A reply can contain fewer than `min_count` messages when the wait ends. The first message can exceed `max_bytes` and return alone, so a large message does not prevent progress. Treat the byte budget as a batching limit, not an absolute allocation guarantee.

## Read several partitions

A partition reader groups targets by their current primary and uses FetchMessages. Each fetch applies `count`, `min_count` and `max_bytes` across its targets together. The reader can keep several fetches active. It can return a partition with messages without waiting for a quiet partition first.

A group consumer uses its assigned partitions. Assignment changes and primary changes require a refresh before further reads. Use the SDK reader or consumer to manage this state. A raw fetch caller must also supply the route and ownership information required by the protocol.

## Choose when to commit

| Policy | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Manual | The application stores checkpoints after successful processing |
| On read | The server submits the last returned offset as part of the read |
| Automatic | A reader or consumer tracks progress and stores it by interval or message count |

A one-shot poll rejects an automatic policy because it has no continuing processing state. On-read commits can precede application processing. A failover before offset replication can also deliver the last batch again. Use manual commits or automatic commits after processing when messages must be processed before their offsets advance.

The Rust automatic policy defaults to every 10,000 messages or five seconds, whichever happens first, after processing. It also stores progress on close, shutdown and partition revocation. Processing counts when the application requests the next item, a handler succeeds, or the reader closes. Marked progress supports applications that finish work concurrently. Do not close a reader as if processing succeeded after a failed handler.

## Cancellation and uncertain results

Cancellation removes a parked request when the server receives it. If a committing poll loses its reply, the client cannot assume that its offset stayed unchanged. SDK recovery tracks the uncertain operation and blocks conflicting work until the application resolves or abandons it. Abandoning permits later work but does not undo an offset that already committed.

## HTTP reads

Use `GET /streams/{stream_id}/topics/{topic_id}/messages/deferred` for a deferred read without offset commits. A read that sets `auto_commit=true` must use `POST` on that path. The server rejects a committing `GET`.

Raw HTTP defaults differ from `PollOptions`: count is 10, wait is one second, and request timeout is 11 seconds. Minimum count is one and the byte budget is 1 MiB.

The query uses `wait_us`, `min_count`, `max_bytes` and `request_timeout_us` alongside the normal consumer, partition, strategy and count fields. A positive wait needs at least one second between the wait and request timeout. Configure a proxy timeout long enough to receive the reply.

## Server capacity

The [sharding configuration](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/server/configuration#sharding) bounds parked requests, per-session requests, disk reads and completion delivery. HTTP requests without a binary session count against their user. Capacity exhaustion can return a retryable error. Keep retries within a bounded application deadline.

---

# Idempotent Producers

> Prevent duplicate appends of a retried producer batch and understand the limits of that guarantee.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/idempotent-producers/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/idempotent-producers.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

An idempotent producer lets a partition recognize a batch it already accepted. Each batch carries a producer ID, epoch and sequence. This identity survives a reconnect under a new client session. It is separate from the ID field of an individual message.

## Rust producer

The Rust high-level producer supports opt-in idempotence on binary transports:

```rust
use iggy::prelude::*;
use std::str::FromStr;

let producer = client.producer("orders", "created")?.idempotent().build();
producer.init().await?;
producer.send_one(IggyMessage::from_str("order-created")?).await?;
producer.shutdown().await;
```

The fragment assumes a connected `IggyClient` in an async function. Initialization obtains the producer ID. The producer selects each chunk's partition and sends chunks for that partition in sequence. The default producer does not enable this mode.

Do not treat a message ID as a deduplication key. Recreating a producer or submitting the same business event as a new batch is not the same as retrying the original producer batch. Consumers still need application-level handling for repeated work.

## Kafka gateway

Set `IGGY_KAFKA_IDEMPOTENT_PRODUCERS=true` on the Kafka gateway to enable its idempotent producer path. The bridge must also be enabled. The default is false. Without this switch, a Kafka producer can obtain an ID but its retries do not receive the batch deduplication guarantee.

The gateway does not support transactions. Idempotent appends do not make application processing and offset commits one atomic operation. See [Kafka gateway](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/gateways/kafka).

## Retained producer history

Each partition retains the last five batches of each producer and at most 4096 producers. A producer idle for 24 hours can expire. A retry outside this retained history can append a duplicate. These limits also apply to the gateway and source connector paths.

## Compatibility and recovery

Upgrade every reader of the topic to a compatible 0.10 client before writing producer-aware batches. The batch format contains additional producer fields. The older SDKs cannot safely decode it.

Session retry protection and producer idempotence solve different problems. A client can retain an uncertain request and resolve it using its original identity. Ending that session can remove receipt access. An idempotent producer adds batch identity at the partition level, but does not turn an uncertain application operation into a confirmed success.

---

# Metadata Changes

> Follow resource and activity changes, retain a position and rebuild after history expires.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/metadata-changes/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/metadata-changes.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The metadata change log records public results of committed metadata operations. It includes resource changes, permissions, sessions and consumer group membership. Reading it requires root or the global `manage_servers` permission.

## Select a starting point

| Start | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Earliest | Read the oldest retained changes |
| Latest | Establish a position at the current end |
| After | Continue after a saved cursor |
| Current | Read pages of current state before following changes |

A cursor identifies a position in this log. Save the returned `next` value after applying the corresponding records. Cursor text starts with `mc1_`. Current-state page tokens start with `cs1_`. Treat both as opaque values and use the SDK parsers.

Queries can select resource or activity groups. Current-state queries must include parent groups, such as streams when topics are selected. Limits range from 1 through 1000. Time bounds are not valid with Latest or Current starts.

## Handle each response

| Status | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Ok | Apply records or current items and save the returned position |
| Behind | Wait and retry without advancing the position |
| Expired | Rebuild because the requested history is no longer retained |
| Reset | Rebuild because the cursor belongs to a different history |

A rebuild reads Current pages, then follows changes from the returned anchor. Keep the rebuilt state private until a change page reports no more records and reaches at least the last current page's `head_op`. A sequence of current pages alone does not establish that the mirror caught up.

Unknown record kinds retain their codes and raw bodies. Stop without advancing the cursor when the application cannot apply a record. Skipping it can leave a mirror inconsistent. Key material is never exposed in stream records. Their public options contain only the key source and fingerprints.

## SDK methods

| SDK | Method |
| --- | --- |
| Rust | `get_metadata_changes` |
| Python | `get_metadata_changes` |
| Node.js | `system.getMetadataChanges` |
| Go | `GetMetadataChanges` |
| Java | `getMetadataChanges` on the system client |
| C# | `GetMetadataChangesAsync` |
| C++ | `GetMetadataChanges` |
| PHP | `getMetadataChanges` |
| Swift | `getMetadataChanges` |

The [Python implementation example](https://github.com/apache/iggy/blob/server-0.10.0-rc.1/foreign/python/README.md#metadata-changes) shows follow and rebuild loops. The other SDK source guides show their equivalent typed queries.

## Retention and node freshness

`metadata.change_log_resource_capacity` defaults to 65536 records. `metadata.change_log_activity_capacity` defaults to 16384 records. Each budget also limits record bodies to 128 MiB. A busy activity log does not evict resource history. Nodes can retain different depths.

A node can lag behind the metadata primary. A cursor that is valid elsewhere can receive Behind from that node. Wait or use a node that has caught up. Expired and Reset require rebuilding, not a loop over the same stale position.

---

# Intro

> The Rust SDK, the primary and most complete Iggy client, and where its source lives.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/intro/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/rust/intro.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

The Rust SDK is the primary and most feature-complete client for Iggy. It is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/iggy) and the source code is part of the [core repository](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/core/sdk).

Run from your application crate to add the published SDK:

```bash
cargo add iggy@0.12.0
```

Use an SDK release compatible with your server. For unreleased changes, build both from the same checkout. The [Getting Started](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/introduction/getting-started) guide shows the source dependency setup.

## Prerequisites

The examples below log in with `iggy`/`iggy`. For a new local development instance, with no `IGGY_ROOT_USERNAME` or `IGGY_ROOT_PASSWORD` overrides, use:

```bash
cargo run --bin iggy-server -- --fresh --with-default-root-credentials
```

`--fresh` **wipes this replica's local data directory**. Environment credentials take precedence over the flag, and bootstrap settings do not replace recovered credentials. In a cluster, a fresh replica can recover credentials from peers. Use disposable development data. A fresh server requires explicit credentials or the development flag.

## High-level vs low-level API

The SDK provides two layers. The snippets below assume an async Tokio context with a `Result` return type.

**High-level API (recommended)** - the easiest way to get started. It handles connection management, auto-batching, consumer group lifecycle, offset commits, retry logic, and reconnection out of the box. Use `IggyClient`, `IggyProducer`, and `IggyConsumer` for the best developer experience.

```rust
use iggy::prelude::*;

// Connect with a connection string
let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")?;
client.connect().await?;

// Or use the builder
let client = IggyClientBuilder::new()
    .with_tcp()
    .with_server_address("127.0.0.1:8090".to_string())
    .build()?;
client.connect().await?;
client.login_user("iggy", "iggy").await?;
```

**Low-level API** - direct access to individual protocol operations. Useful when you need fine-grained control over every request, or when building custom abstractions on top.

The high-level API is built on top of the low-level one, so you can always drop down when needed.

## Connection string

The connection string is the simplest way to configure the client. It supports all four transport protocols:

```text
iggy://user:pass@host:port              (TCP, default)
iggy+tcp://user:pass@host:port          (TCP, explicit)
iggy+quic://user:pass@host:port         (QUIC)
iggy+http://user:pass@host:port         (HTTP)
iggy+ws://user:pass@host:port           (WebSocket)
```

TCP, QUIC, and WebSocket apply connection-string credentials on `connect()`. HTTP requires an explicit login and supports ordinary consumers only.

Options can be appended as query parameters:

```text
iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090?nodelay=true&heartbeat_interval=5s
iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090?reconnection_retries=unlimited&heartbeat_interval=5s
```

Personal Access Tokens are also supported. Any credential without a colon is treated as a PAT. Paste the token exactly as the server returned it, with **no prefix**:

```text
iggy://<personal-access-token>@127.0.0.1:8090
```

See [Connection Strings](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/connection-strings) for the full per-transport option tables and defaults.

## Quick example

```rust
use iggy::prelude::*;
use std::str::FromStr;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let client = IggyClient::from_connection_string("iggy://iggy:iggy@127.0.0.1:8090")?;
    client.connect().await?;

    // Re-running this example is fine: an existing stream or topic is not an error.
    match client.create_stream("my-stream", &StreamCreateOptions::default()).await {
        Ok(_) | Err(IggyError::StreamNameAlreadyExists(_)) => {}
        Err(e) => return Err(e.into()),
    }
    // Every topic knob rides `TopicCreateOptions`. Fields left as `None`
    // resolve against the server's defaults at admission.
    match client
        .create_topic(
            &"my-stream".try_into()?,
            "my-topic",
            &TopicCreateOptions {
                partitions_count: Some(1),
                message_expiry: Some(IggyExpiry::NeverExpire),
                ..TopicCreateOptions::default()
            },
        )
        .await
    {
        Ok(_) | Err(IggyError::TopicNameAlreadyExists(_, _)) => {}
        Err(e) => return Err(e.into()),
    }

    let msg = IggyMessage::from_str("hello world")?;
    client
        .send_messages(
            &"my-stream".try_into()?,
            &"my-topic".try_into()?,
            &Partitioning::partition_id(0),
            &mut [msg],
        )
        .await?;
    println!("Message sent");

    let polled = client
        .poll_messages(
            &"my-stream".try_into()?,
            &"my-topic".try_into()?,
            0,
            &Consumer::default(),
            &PollingStrategy::next(),
            PollOptions {
                count: 10,
                commit: CommitPolicy::OnRead,
                ..PollOptions::default()
            },
        )
        .await?;

    for message in &polled.messages {
        let payload = std::str::from_utf8(&message.payload)?;
        println!("Offset: {}, Payload: {}", message.header.offset, payload);
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

Partition IDs are **0-based**: the first partition of a topic is partition `0`. The consumer uses the default consumer identity and requests auto-commit. Its offset can advance before application processing finishes. Use explicit offset storage after successful processing when that distinction matters.

For the full getting started tutorial, see [Getting Started](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/introduction/getting-started). For the high-level producer/consumer builders, see [High-level SDK](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/high-level-sdk) and [Stream Builder](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/stream-builder).

---

# Examples

> The Rust SDK examples in the core repository, and how to start a server to run them against.

Rendered page: https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/examples/

Source: https://github.com/apache/iggy-website/blob/main/content/docs/sdk/rust/examples.mdx

Docs version: server 0.10.0, Rust SDK 0.12.0, CLI 0.15.0, Node.js SDK 0.11.0, Python, Java, Go and C# SDKs 0.10.0, Swift, C++ and PHP SDKs 0.2.0

In the core repository, you can find the following [examples](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src) using the Rust SDK.

Build the SDK and server from the same checkout for unreleased changes. Start the server from the repository root in a separate terminal. The examples use `iggy`/`iggy`. For a new local instance with no `IGGY_ROOT_USERNAME` or `IGGY_ROOT_PASSWORD` overrides:

```bash
cargo run --bin iggy-server -- --fresh --with-default-root-credentials
```

Environment credentials take precedence over the flag, and bootstrap settings do not replace recovered credentials. `--fresh` deletes this replica's local data. Use disposable development data. A new standalone server without explicit credentials generates a root password. A new cluster requires explicit credentials.

The examples are cargo example targets of the `iggy_examples` crate. Run them from the **repository root** with `cargo run --example <name>` so relative certificate paths resolve. Run each producer before its consumer. Some examples create fixed names and require fresh data when repeated. The getting-started consumer also expects stream and topic IDs `0`, so run that pair first on a fresh server. Partition IDs are **0-based**, but balanced producers and consumer groups can use multiple partitions.

- **[Getting started](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/getting-started)** - the basic example which is discussed in the [getting started](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/introduction/getting-started) guide.

  ```bash
  cargo run --example getting-started-producer
  cargo run --example getting-started-consumer
  ```

- **[Basic](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/basic)** - producer and consumer using the low-level `Client` trait with CLI args for transport selection (TCP/QUIC/HTTP/WebSocket).

  ```bash
  cargo run --example basic-producer
  cargo run --example basic-consumer
  ```

- **[New SDK](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/new-sdk)** - an introduction to the high-level SDK as discussed in the [dedicated guide](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/high-level-sdk).

  ```bash
  cargo run --example new-sdk-producer
  cargo run --example new-sdk-consumer
  ```

- **[Stream builder](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/stream-builder)** - examples using the `IggyStream`, `IggyStreamProducer`, and `IggyStreamConsumer` builder APIs as discussed in the [stream builder guide](https://iggy.apache.org/docs/sdk/rust/stream-builder).

  ```bash
  cargo run --example stream-basic
  cargo run --example stream-producer
  cargo run --example stream-consumer
  cargo run --example stream-producer-config
  cargo run --example stream-consumer-config
  ```

- **[Message envelope](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/message-envelope)** - the example of how to send a message with a custom envelope e.g. to differentiate between different types of messages.

  ```bash
  cargo run --example message-envelope-producer
  cargo run --example message-envelope-consumer
  ```

- **[Message headers](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/message-headers)** - the example of how to send a message with custom headers (typed headers, message type discrimination, client-side compression).

  ```bash
  cargo run --example message-headers-type-producer
  cargo run --example message-headers-type-consumer
  cargo run --example message-headers-compression-producer
  cargo run --example message-headers-compression-consumer
  cargo run --example typed-headers-producer
  cargo run --example typed-headers-consumer
  ```

- **[Multi-tenant](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/multi-tenant)** - the larger example of how to structure your application to support multiple tenants (separated by the unique streams) with the different users, permissions, topics etc.

  ```bash
  cargo run --example multi-tenant-producer
  cargo run --example multi-tenant-consumer
  ```

- **[TCP TLS](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/tcp-tls)** - TLS-encrypted TCP connections with custom CA certificates. Stop the plain server and start a TLS-enabled server from the repository root:

  ```bash
  IGGY_TCP_TLS_ENABLED=true \
  IGGY_TCP_TLS_CERT_FILE=core/certs/iggy_cert.pem \
  IGGY_TCP_TLS_KEY_FILE=core/certs/iggy_key.pem \
  cargo run --bin iggy-server -- --fresh --with-default-root-credentials
  ```

These certificates are for local testing. Then run:

  ```bash
  cargo run --example tcp-tls-producer
  cargo run --example tcp-tls-consumer
  ```

- **[Sink data producer](https://github.com/apache/iggy/tree/server-0.10.0-rc.1/examples/rust/src/sink-data-producer)** - generating random JSON records in bulk batches for sink connector testing.

  ```bash
  cargo run --example sink-data-producer
  ```
